title: Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (ZeRO & FSDP): How Sharding Optimizer States, Gradients, and Parameters Breaks the LLM Memory Wall
summary: When training modern large language models, static memory consumption is dominated not by the model weights themselves, but by the optimizer states: FP32 Adam master weights, momentum, and variance consume 12 bytes per parameter—three times more memory than the FP16 weights and gradients combined. In standard Distributed Data Parallelism (DDP), every GPU maintains an identical copy of these states, causing GPUs to run out of memory before training even begins. Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) and DeepSpeed ZeRO eliminate this redundancy by partitioning optimizer states, gradients, and model parameters across data-parallel ranks. By streaming sharded weights on-demand during forward and backward passes via All-Gather and immediately releasing them, ZeRO-3 achieves linear memory scaling across the GPU cluster while overlapping communication with computation to preserve peak training throughput.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Pit Crew Tool Warehouse vs. The On-Demand Tool Caddy
analogy:
Imagine a high-performance 8-mechanic pit crew servicing race cars during an endurance championship. The complete master toolkit—heavy hydraulic lifts, engine calibration stations, torque wrenches, tire warmers, and telemetry analyzers—weighs 1,600 kilograms.

Under Classic Data Parallelism (DDP), every single mechanic straps the entire 1,600 kg warehouse onto their back. Even though a mechanic only needs a torque wrench for five seconds during tire changes and the heavy calibration computers are only turned on once per lap, every worker carries duplicate copies of every single machine at every moment. The mechanics collapse under the crushing weight before the race even begins.

Under ZeRO-1 (Optimizer State Sharding), the team realizes that the heavy calibration computers (the 12-byte Adam states, which represent 75% of the total load) don't need to be duplicated. They divide the machines among the crew: Mechanic 1 holds the tire balancer, Mechanic 2 holds the telemetry terminal. Each mechanic's load instantly drops from 1,600 kg to 500 kg, while keeping their everyday tools handy.

Under ZeRO-3 / FSDP (Full Parameter Sharding), the crew eliminates all remaining redundancy. No mechanic carries even the full set of everyday wrenches! Mechanic 1 holds the 10mm sockets, Mechanic 2 holds the 14mm sockets. When Mechanic 1 needs to tighten a front wing bolt on Lap 4, Mechanic 2 passes the socket over on-demand (an All-Gather). As soon as the bolt is torqued, Mechanic 1 passes it back and frees their hands. By sharing tools in micro-second handoffs only when a specific task is actively executing, each mechanic carries just 1/8th of the weight, enabling the crew to handle massive equipment without breaking their backs.

sections.heading: 1. The 16-Byte-Per-Parameter Wall: Why Classic DDP Runs Out of Memory
sections.content:
In deep learning, Distributed Data Parallelism (DDP) is the most intuitive distributed paradigm: every GPU hosts an identical copy of the model, a global mini-batch is partitioned across GPUs, and each GPU independently computes forward activations and backward gradients on its local slice of data. At the end of the backward pass, an All-Reduce synchronizes the gradients across all devices, and every GPU updates its weights.

However, when scaling to large language models, DDP collides with a mathematical memory wall. In mixed-precision training (FP16 or BF16), model memory divides into static memory and dynamic activation memory. Static memory per parameter $\Psi$ consists of three distinct buckets:

• Model Parameters: 2 bytes per parameter (in FP16/BF16).
• Gradients: 2 bytes per parameter (in FP16/BF16).
• Optimizer States (Adam): To prevent underflow and numerical instability during weight updates, the Adam optimizer maintains three FP32 tensors for every single parameter: an FP32 master weight (4 bytes), FP32 momentum / first moment (4 bytes), and FP32 variance / second moment (4 bytes). That is 12 bytes per parameter in optimizer states alone!

Summing these up yields $2 + 2 + 12 = 16$ bytes per parameter. For a 70-billion-parameter model, static memory demands $70 \times 10^9 \times 16 \text{ bytes} = 1,120 \text{ GB}$ (1.12 Terabytes) of VRAM. An 80 GB NVIDIA H100 cannot even fit 10% of this static requirement. Under standard DDP, every GPU in a cluster of 64 GPUs holds this identical 1.12 TB state—a 64-fold duplication of memory that wastes terabytes of expensive High Bandwidth Memory (HBM).

sections.heading: 2. The Three Stages of ZeRO: Sharding States, Gradients, and Parameters
sections.content:
The Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO), pioneered by Microsoft DeepSpeed and standardized in PyTorch as Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP), eliminates this duplication. Instead of replicating identical memory across all $N_{DP}$ data-parallel ranks, ZeRO partitions the memory across the devices while retaining the computational simplicity of data parallelism through three progressive stages:

• ZeRO-Stage 1 ($P_{os}$ — Optimizer State Sharding):
The 12-byte Adam optimizer states are partitioned equally across the $N$ GPUs. Each GPU stores only $\frac{12\Psi}{N}$ bytes of optimizer states. During the backward pass, each GPU computes local gradients for all parameters. After an All-Reduce averages the gradients, GPU $i$ updates only its assigned $\frac{1}{N}$ slice of the FP32 master weights. It converts the updated parameters back to FP16, and an All-Gather broadcasts the updated parameters to all GPUs. For $N=64$, static memory drops from 16 bytes/param to $4 + \frac{12}{64} \approx 4.19$ bytes/param—a 4x memory reduction with zero increase in total communication volume.

• ZeRO-Stage 2 ($P_{os+g}$ — Gradient Sharding):
Gradients are also partitioned. As backpropagation unwinds layer by layer from the model output to the input, gradients for layer $L$ are generated. Instead of running a full All-Reduce (which produces a full copy of gradients on every GPU), the GPUs execute a Reduce-Scatter. Each GPU only receives and accumulates the gradients corresponding to its assigned parameter partition. Once reduced, the remaining local gradients are freed immediately. Static memory drops to $2 + \frac{14}{N} \approx 2.22$ bytes/param—an 8x memory reduction, still with the exact same communication volume as standard DDP.

• ZeRO-Stage 3 ($P_{os+g+p}$ — Parameter Sharding / PyTorch FSDP):
The model parameters themselves are partitioned. No GPU stores a complete copy of the model weights. Static memory drops to $\frac{16\Psi}{N}$ bytes per GPU—achieving true linear memory scaling. For 64 GPUs, static memory shrinks to just $0.25$ bytes per parameter, allowing a 70B model to easily fit into 16 or 32 commodity GPUs without complex tensor slicing.

sections.heading: 3. Collective Communication Math, All-Gather Prefetching, and FSDP Overlap
sections.content:
The central question engineers ask when looking at ZeRO-3 / FSDP is: If parameters are sharded, how can a GPU compute matrix multiplications on layers it does not store?

The answer lies in dynamic just-in-time weight streaming orchestrated by collective communication primitives:

• Forward Pass Lifecycle: When the forward pass reaches layer $L$, the GPUs trigger an All-Gather collective. Each GPU sends its local $\frac{1}{N}$ slice of layer $L$'s weights to all other GPUs. Once the full layer weights are reconstructed in temporary memory, the forward GEMM (General Matrix Multiply) executes. The moment the forward step for layer $L$ finishes, the reconstructed weights are immediately freed from VRAM, and the GPU moves to layer $L+1$.
• Backward Pass Lifecycle: During backpropagation, the GPU triggers another All-Gather to rebuild layer $L$'s weights, calculates the input activation gradients and parameter gradients, runs a Reduce-Scatter to send parameter gradients to their respective partition owners, and immediately frees the layer weights once again.

• The Communication Tradeoff: Standard DDP transfers $2\Psi$ of data during gradient All-Reduce. ZeRO-3 transfers $1\Psi$ (Forward All-Gather) + $1\Psi$ (Backward All-Gather) + $1\Psi$ (Backward Reduce-Scatter) = $3\Psi$. This represents a 50% communication increase over standard DDP.

• Hiding Latency with CUDA Stream Overlapping (Prefetching): PyTorch FSDP hides this 50% overhead completely using dual CUDA streams. While the GPU tensor cores execute matrix multiplication for layer $L$ on the primary computation stream, the communication stream asynchronously issues the non-blocking All-Gather for layer $L+1$ across the high-speed network fabric (InfiniBand or RoCE). By the time layer $L$ finishes, layer $L+1$'s weights are already resident in cache. In production clusters with sufficient interconnect bandwidth, ZeRO-3 achieves near-identical computational efficiency to standard DDP while training models orders of magnitude larger.

takeaway: Classic Data Parallelism fails on modern LLMs because each GPU duplicates optimizer states, gradients, and parameters—wasting over 75% of VRAM on identical FP32 Adam states. ZeRO and PyTorch FSDP eliminate this redundancy by sharding states (ZeRO-1), gradients (ZeRO-2), and parameters (ZeRO-3) across the data-parallel cluster. By streaming weights on-demand layer-by-layer via All-Gather and overlapping communication with computation, FSDP delivers linear memory scaling with cluster size, enabling teams to train massive models without out-of-memory bottlenecks.
